evidence_first_authors: DuBose et al., Harfouche et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Rapid access to a clinical team 24/7 competent in haemorrhage control and delivery of both open and endovascular surgery is recommended for the management of patients with life or limb threatening vascular injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Implementation of civilian and military vascular trauma curricula and dedicated training are recommended for the development and maintenance of vascular trauma decision making and technical skills.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Emergency access to an operating room with hybrid capability is recommended for the operative treatment of the trauma patient with a vascular injury.

evidence_first_authors: Holcomb et al., Roberts et al, Sperry et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Damage control resuscitation principles and massive transfusion protocols used for patients with traumatic haemorrhage are recommended for patients with vascular trauma.

evidence_first_authors:
Roberts et al., Fouche et al.,
Asaadi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Early administration of tranexamic acid is recommended for all severely bleeding patients with vascular trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Scerbo et al., Beekley et al., Covey et al., Benitez et al., Henry et al., Teixera et al.
rec_text_verbatim: A pre-hospital tourniquet, applied as distally as possible, is recommended for patients with uncontrolled bleeding from extremity vascular trauma when local compression and or packing are not sufficient.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Heparinisation is not indicated as part of tourniquet management in patients with uncontrolled bleeding from extremity vascular trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Jansen et al., Maiga et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is not recommended as a routine approach for temporary haemorrhage control in trauma patients with exsanguinating torso haemorrhage.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Haemodynamically unstable patients, deemed unsuitable for computed tomography angiography, are recommended to be immediately transferred to the operating room for surgical intervention.

evidence_first_authors: Inaba et al., Patterson et al., Walkoff et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Computed tomography angiography, including arterial and venous phase, is recommended as the first line investigation to identify or rule out vascular injury in trauma patients without clinical signs of active bleeding.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Avoiding or postponing computed tomography angiography because of possible renal impairment is not recommended in haemodynamically stable patients with potentially life or limb threatening vascular injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Alarhayem et al. Vuoncino et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Restoration of inline arterial flow, temporarily or definitively, is recommended to be prioritised in the management of limb or end organ threatening vascular trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Primary definitive repair for patients with vascular trauma is recommended over temporary solutions.

evidence_first_authors: Tung et al., Borut et al., Subramanian et al., Polcz et al., Laverty et al., Feliciano et al.
rec_text_verbatim: The use of temporary vascular shunts to rapidly restore blood flow is recommended when timely primary definitive vascular repair is not feasible due to patient physiology or injury pattern.

evidence_first_authors: Mathew et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Vascular shunts should be considered for conversion to definitive repair as soon as possible, ideally at the primary operation.

evidence_first_authors: Ray et al., Karmy-Jones et al., Aksoy et al., Yagubyan et al., Lyons et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Short interposition grafts are recommended in patients with vascular trauma requiring reconstruction.

evidence_first_authors: Watson et al., Forsyth et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Vein grafts should be considered for vascular reconstruction of arterial injury requiring longer bypass conduits or for small calibre distal vessels.

evidence_first_authors: Hafez et al., Fox et al., Lakhwani et al., Parry et al., Stonko et al., Watson et al., Reilly et al., Ur Rehman
rec_text_verbatim: Synthetic interposition grafts may be considered for emergency definitive vascular repair.

evidence_first_authors: Bell et al., Tisherman et al., Sperry et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Immediate open surgical exploration is recommended for patients with penetrating neck injury and active haemorrhage from the wound or expanding haematoma.

evidence_first_authors: Patterson et al., Karagiorgas et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Computed tomography angiography is recommended for all patients with penetrating neck trauma without an indication for immediate operative intervention.

evidence_first_authors: Weinberg et al., Ronaldi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with single antiplatelet therapy may be considered for patients with minor (ESVS Grade 1) carotid artery injury due to penetrating trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Plotkin et al., du Toit et al., Reva et al., Madsen et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Reconstruction rather than ligation of the common or internal carotid artery, when patient physiology allows and technically feasible, is recommended in patients with penetrating ESVS Grade 2 or 3 carotid artery injury.

evidence_first_authors: Piper et al., Asensio et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with single antiplatelet therapy may be considered for patients with an ESVS Grade 1 vertebral artery injury due to penetrating trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Piper et al. Asensio et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular therapy should be considered as first line treatment for symptomatic or progressing pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula (ESVS Grade 2) in patients with penetrating vertebral artery injury.

evidence_first_authors: Piper et al., Asensio et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Emergency endovascular management with embolisation if feasible is recommended for patients with penetrating extracranial vertebral artery injury and uncontrolled haemorrhage (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with single antiplatelet therapy should be considered for patients with penetrating extracranial vertebral artery injury and occlusion (ESVS Grade X) without neurological symptoms.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Ligation is recommended if repair of internal jugular vein injury is not easily achievable, provided one internal jugular vein remains patent.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Clinical examination alone is not recommended to rule out cervical vascular injury in patients with blunt neck trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Patterson et al., Karagiorgas et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Computed tomography angiography including intracerebral vessels is recommended for all patients at risk of blunt cerebrovascular injury.

evidence_first_authors: Brommeland et al., Geddes et al., Biffl et al., Biffl et al., Leichtle et al., Jacobson et al., Black et al.
rec_text_verbatim: The use of screening protocols to identify cervical vascular injury early should be considered for patients with blunt trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Russo et al., Brommeland et al., Murphy et al., Shahani et al., Momic et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with single antiplatelet therapy is recommended for patients with blunt, low grade carotid artery injury (ESVS Grade 1).

evidence_first_authors: Russo et al., Weber et al., Brommeland et al., Kim et al.
rec_text_verbatim: The use of routine endovascular stenting as an adjunct to antithrombotic therapy is not recommended for patients with blunt carotid artery injury without active bleeding (ESVS Grade 1 or 2).

evidence_first_authors: Lauerman et al., Shahah et al., Mei et al., Burlew et al., DiCocco et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Delayed endovascular treatment may be considered for patients with blunt carotid or vertebral artery injury and enlarging pseudoaneurysm (ESVS Grade 2) or neurological symptoms.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Operative treatment with open repair or endovascular stent graft is recommended for patients with blunt carotid artery injury and active haemorrhage (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with single antiplatelet therapy should be considered for patients with blunt carotid injury and complete occlusion (ESVS Grade X) without neurological symptoms.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Management of blunt carotid injury and complete occlusion (ESVS Grade X) with neurological symptoms should be considered on an individual basis, including the duration of neurological symptoms, risk of reperfusion injury, and signs of brain infarction on computed tomography.

evidence_first_authors: Markus et al., Rosati et al., Patel et al., Daou et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Management with antiplatelet therapy as first line treatment is recommended for patients with blunt vertebral artery injury without active haemorrhage (ESVS Grades 1, 2, or X).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Emergency endovascular management with embolisation, if feasible, is recommended for patients with blunt extracranial vertebral artery injury and uncontrolled haemorrhage (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Surveillance with computed tomography angiography at one week and three months should be considered for patients with blunt carotid artery injury (ESVS Grade 1 or 2) undergoing non-operative management with antiplatelet treatment.

evidence_first_authors: Fabian et al., Neschis et al., Bossone et al., Gaffey et al., Osgood et al., Jacob-Brassard et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Systolic blood pressure (90 – 110 mmHg) and heart rate (<100/minute) control are recommended for patients with untreated blunt thoracic aortic injury except in the presence of hypovolaemic shock or traumatic brain injury.

evidence_first_authors: Ultee et al., Mohapatra et al., MacKenzie et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Referral to a trauma centre with 24/7 multispecialty expertise to treat aortic pathology is recommended for all patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury.

evidence_first_authors: Bruckner et al., Gutierrez et al., Downing et al., Ho et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Chest Xray is not recommended as an imaging technique to exclude blunt thoracic aortic injury.

evidence_first_authors: Bruckner et al., Katayama et al., Gutierrez et al., Fabian et al., Patterson et al., Ho et al., Fox et al., Evangelista et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Computed tomography angiography of the aorta is recommended for the diagnosis and characterisation of blunt thoracic aortic injury.

evidence_first_authors: Yadavalli et al., Jacob-Brassard et al., Soong et al., Fox et al., Demetriades et al., Alarhayem et al., Harris et al., DuBose et al., Starnes et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with blood pressure control and follow up imaging is recommended in patients with ESVS Grade 1 blunt thoracic aortic injury without concomitant severe traumatic brain injury.

evidence_first_authors: Rabin et al., Arbabi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair may be considered in patients with ESVS Grade 1 blunt thoracic aortic injury and concomitant severe traumatic brain injury when blood pressure control is not feasible.

evidence_first_authors: Yadavalli et al., Jacob-Brassard et al., Soong et al., Fox et al., Marcaccio et al., McCurdy et al., Romijn et al., Zambetti et al., Alarhayem et al., Demetriades et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Delayed (> 24 hour) endovascular stent graft repair should be considered for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury and any external wall contour abnormality (ESVS Grade 2) if there are no high risk injury features.\*

evidence_first_authors: DuBose et al., Yadavalli et al., Jacob-Brassard et al., Soong et al., Fox et al., Marcaccio et al., Romijn et al., Alarhayem et al., Harris et al., Starnes et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Urgent (<24 hour) endovascular stent graft repair is recommended for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury and any external contour abnormality (ESVS Grade 2) with high risk aortic features.*

evidence_first_authors: Yadavalli et al., Jacob-Brassard et al., Soong et al., Fox et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Immediate operative repair is recommended for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury with active extravasation (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Intra-operative systemic heparinisation for thoracic aortic stent graft repair should be considered individualised, including the perceived risks of bleeding, thromboembolic complications, and severity of traumatic brain injury.

evidence_first_authors: Jonker et al., Muhs et al., Ceja-Rodriguez et al., García Reyes et al., Mesar et al., Bae and Jeon, Gennai et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Stent graft oversizing between 20% and 30%, depending on the hypovolaemic status during index computed tomography angiography, should be considered for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury undergoing emergency endovascular treatment.

evidence_first_authors: Kritayakirana et al., Chen et al., Sepehripour et al., Rizvi et al., Matsumura et al., van der Zee et al., Romagnoli et al., Kruger et al., McBride et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Routine left subclavian artery revascularisation is not indicated for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury requiring endovascular stent graft repair with coverage of the left subclavian artery.

evidence_first_authors: Kritayakirana et al., Chen et al., Sepehripour et al., Rizvi et al., Matsumura et al., van der Zee et al., Romagnoli et al., Kruger et al., McBride et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Left subclavian artery revascularisation is recommended for selected patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury requiring endovascular stent graft repair with coverage of the left subclavian artery and risk of compromised perfusion to brain, heart, or spinal cord.

evidence_first_authors: Kritayakirana et al., Chen et al., Sepehripour et al., Rizvi et al., Matsumura et al., van der Zee et al., Romagnoli et al., Kruger et al., McBride et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Delayed left subclavian artery revascularisation should be considered for selected patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury requiring endovascular stent graft repair who develop ischaemic symptoms with coverage of the left subclavian artery.

evidence_first_authors: Fabian et al., Demetriades et al., Estrera et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Open surgical repair is recommended in selected patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury requiring intervention and with an aortic anatomy unsuitable for a stent graft.

evidence_first_authors: Fabian et al., Demetriades et al., Estrera et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Active distal aortic perfusion is recommended to minimise the risk of paraplegia for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury undergoing open surgical repair.

evidence_first_authors: Guala et al., Khoyezhad et al., Canaud et al., Spiliotopoulos et al., Steuer et al., Gennai et al., Makalovski et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Follow up imaging is recommended for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury who have undergone endovascular stent graft repair, at one month, one year, and thereafter continued for at least five years.

evidence_first_authors: Jacob-Brassard et al., Arbabi et al., Soong et al., Mosquera et al., Madigan et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Surveillance imaging until aortic remodelling is recommended for patients with blunt thoracic aortic injury who have not undergone thoracic aortic repair.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Magnetic resonance angiography is recommended as the preferred imaging method for long term surveillance after blunt thoracic aortic injury.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: The treatment choice of open surgical or endovascular repair of innominate artery or proximal left common carotid artery injury (ESVS Grade 2 and 3) should be considered based on haemodynamic status, anatomy, and concomitant injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Branco et al., Zambetti et al., DuBose et al., Waller et al., Hanif et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair should be considered the preferred treatment modality for patients with subclavian artery injury (ESVS Grade 2 and 3) requiring operative treatment.

evidence_first_authors: Sorrentino et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Immediate surgical exploration and haemorrhage control are recommended for patients in shock with ongoing bleeding and suspicion of major abdominal vascular injury.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Surgical exploration of retroperitoneal haematomas during trauma laparotomy is recommended in patients who are haemodynamically unstable OR who have an unstable retroperitoneal haematoma (expanding, pulsatile, or actively bleeding).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: A non-exploratory approach of retroperitoneal haematomas during trauma laparotomy, with subsequent computed tomography angiography imaging, is recommended for patients who are haemodynamically stable AND have a stable retroperitoneal haematoma (not expanding, not pulsatile, and not actively bleeding).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with surveillance and antithrombotic therapy is recommended for patients without ongoing bleeding and blunt minor abdominal aortic, iliac, renal, or superior mesenteric artery injuries (ESVS Grade 1) on computed tomography angiography.

evidence_first_authors: Shallhub et al., Charlton-Ouw et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Open surgical repair is recommended as first line treatment for patients with blunt or penetrating abdominal aortic injury with free haemorrhage and haemodynamic instability (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Synthetic graft material is recommended for aortic reconstruction in emergency situations with or without concomitant bowel injury.

evidence_first_authors: Shalhub et al., Dayama et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair should be considered for haemodynamically stable patients and abdominal aortic injury with external contour abnormality such as a pseudoaneurysm (ESVS Grade 2).

evidence_first_authors: Jonker et al., Ceja-Rodriguez et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Stent graft oversizing between 20% and 30% should be considered when imaging was performed during hypotension for patients with abdominal aortic injury undergoing emergency endovascular treatment.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Primary surgical repair, synthetic interposition graft reconstruction, or vascular shunting is recommended for common or external iliac artery injury (ESVS Grade 3) discovered during emergency laparotomy.

evidence_first_authors: Kufner et al., Ruffino et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair should be considered for ESVS Grade 2 or 3 common or external iliac artery injury.

evidence_first_authors: Velmahos et al., Fu et al., Bonde et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular treatment with embolisation is recommended for patients with pelvic injury and clinical signs of ongoing bleeding or imaging showing extravasation from the internal iliac artery or its branches.

evidence_first_authors: Maithel et al., Evans et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent or stent graft repair may be considered for ESVS Grade X superior mesenteric artery injury to achieve early restoration of bowel perfusion.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Ligation is recommended for treatment of inferior mesenteric artery injury.

evidence_first_authors: Ouriel et al., Hass et al., Jawas et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Revascularisation of a devascularised unilateral kidney identified on computed tomography angiography is not recommended.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Open or endovascular renal artery repair should be considered for haemodynamically stable patients and ESVS Grade 3 renal artery injury.

evidence_first_authors: Santucci et al., Morey et al., Knudson et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Ligation of the renal artery, with or without simultaneous nephrectomy, is recommended in a haemodynamically unstable patient with severe renal artery injury (ESVS Grade 3).

evidence_first_authors: Liguori et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair should be considered for haemodynamically stable patients with ESVS Grade 2 injury (e.g., pseudoaneurysm) of the renal artery.

evidence_first_authors: Santucci et al., Knudson et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Open or endovascular renal artery repair is recommended for patients with bilateral ESVS Grade 2, 3, or X renal artery injuries or if there is a solitary salvageable kidney.

evidence_first_authors: Balachandran et al., Stonko et al., Navsaria et al., Matsumoto et al., Howley et al., Asensio et al., Asensio et al., Ksycki et al., Magee et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Vein ligation is recommended for abdominal venous injury if repair is not easily achievable.

evidence_first_authors: Pinto et al., Choi et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with close observation and follow up imaging should be considered in haemodynamically stable patients with inferior vena cava injury and a stable retroperitoneal haematoma (not expanding and not actively bleeding).

evidence_first_authors: Sullivan et al., Zargarani et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Atrio caval shunting is not indicated in the management of inferior vena cava injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Abou-Sayed et al., Inaba et al., Joseph et al., Le Roux et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Careful clinical vascular examination is recommended in all patients with extremity trauma to identify potential haemorrhagic or ischaemic vascular injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Abou-Sayed et al., Inaba et al., Joseph et al., Le Roux et al.
rec_text_verbatim: An ankle brachial index is not indicated to diagnose or rule out vascular injury in patients with extremity trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Adibi et al., Branco et al., Jens et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Immediate computed tomography angiography is recommended as the primary imaging modality in patients with extremity injury where significant vascular injury cannot be ruled out by clinical vascular examination (palpable peripheral pulses).

evidence_first_authors: Alarhayem et al., Perkins et al., Glass et al., Perkins et al., Ray et al., Zaraca et al., Hsieh et al., Chipman et al., Lewis Jr et al., Magnotti et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Revascularisation as soon as possible, ideally within one hour of admission, is recommended in patients with clinical evidence of acute ischaemia due to extremity vascular trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Tung et al., Borut et al., Subramanian et al., Polcz et al., Laverty et al., Feliciano et al.
rec_text_verbatim: The use of a temporary vascular shunt to rapidly restore blood flow in the extremity is recommended when timely primary definitive vascular repair is not feasible due to patient physiology or skeletal instability.

evidence_first_authors: Schirò et al., Loja et al., Elshawary, Nayar et al., Prichayudh et al., Yoneda et al., Gratl et al.
rec_text_verbatim: The use of scoring systems when deciding upon limb salvage or amputation for patients with extremity trauma is not recommended.

evidence_first_authors: Schirò et al., Loja et al., Elshawary, Nayar et al., Prichayudh et al., Yoneda et al., Gratl et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Multidisciplinary decision making regarding revascularisation vs. primary amputation is recommended in patients with complex extremity trauma.

evidence_first_authors: Dennis et al., Pan et al., Frykberg et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management with clinical and imaging follow up may be considered for patients with extremity non-occlusive vascular injuries (ESVS Grade 1 or 2).

evidence_first_authors: Asmar et al., Butler et al., Wormi et al., Magee et al., Potter et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent or stent graft repair may be considered as an alternative to open repair in selected patients with extremity vascular trauma requiring operative treatment (ESVS Grade 2, 3, or X).

evidence_first_authors: Maleux et al., D'Alessio et al., Cheraghali et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular embolisation is recommended for active bleeding from side branches of major arteries in patients with extremity injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Schippers et al.
rec_text_verbatim: If repair is not easily achievable, ligation is recommended in isolated radial or ulnar arterial injury without evidence of distal ischaemia.

evidence_first_authors: Lee et al., Dua et al., Croman et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Ligation or embolisation of an isolated infragenicular arterial injury without evidence of distal ischaemia may be considered in patients with one of the anterior or posterior tibial arteries intact and patent.

evidence_first_authors: Guerrero et al., Maher et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Intra-operative systemic heparinisation in patients with extremity trauma may be considered on an individual basis, including the extent of repair, duration of interrupted blood flow, concomitant injuries and overall risk of bleeding, and degree of trauma induced coagulopathy.

evidence_first_authors: O'Shea et al., Byerly et al., Matsumoto et al., Manley et al., Perkins et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Repair of localised femoral or popliteal venous injury should be considered over ligation in haemodynamically stable patients.

evidence_first_authors: von Keudell et al., Farber et al., Bible et al., Etemad-Rezaie et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Emergency four compartment fasciotomy is recommended to treat traumatic post-ischaemic lower limb compartment syndrome.

evidence_first_authors: Dorweiler et al., Abu Dabrh et al., Sarpe et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Post-operative follow up with clinical examination and duplex ultrasound one month after repair, or earlier if abnormal findings or symptoms develop, may be considered for patients with extremity vascular injury and vascular reconstruction.

evidence_first_authors: Khan et al., Stonko et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Post-operative single antiplatelet therapy may be considered for patients with vascular trauma who have undergone open or endovascular repair.

evidence_first_authors: Patterson et al., Moody et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Computed tomography angiography is recommended as the first line investigation to identify or rule out vascular injury in haemodynamically stable paediatric trauma patients.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Early antithrombotic therapy is recommended for children with blunt, low grade carotid artery injury (ESVS Grade 1 or 2).

evidence_first_authors: Hosn et al., Raulli et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Endovascular stent graft repair should be considered as the first line operative treatment for children with blunt thoracic aortic injury (ESVS Grade 2 or 3) and appropriate anatomy.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Immediate surgical exploration and bleeding control are recommended for children in shock with ongoing haemorrhage and suspicion of major abdominal vascular injury.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Clinical vascular examination in line with adult guidance is recommended in all children with upper or lower extremity trauma to identify potential haemorrhagic or ischaemic vascular injuries.

evidence_first_authors: Delniotis et al., Goh et al., Griffin et al.
rec_text_verbatim: Non-operative management should be considered in a child with a pink and warm, but pulseless, hand post-supracondylar humeral fracture reduction with close observation for the development of acute ischaemia.

evidence_first_authors: Consensus
rec_text_verbatim: Post-operative follow up with clinical examination and duplex ultrasound one month after repair, or earlier if abnormal findings or symptoms develop, may be considered for children with extremity vascular injury reconstructed with bypass or interposition graft.
